title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Definition of a Group
A group \((G,\cdot)\) is a set \(G\) together with a law of composition
\((a,b)\mapsto a\cdot b\) satisfying:

Associativity:
\((a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)\) for \(a,b,c\in G\).
Identity:
There exists \(e\in G\) such that \(e\cdot a=a\cdot e=a\) for every \(a\in G\).
Inverses:
For each \(a\in G\), there exists \(a^{-1}\in G\) such that \(a\cdot a^{-1}=a^{-1}\cdot a=e\).
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Definition of a Subgroup
Let \(G\) be a group.
A subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) is a subset \(H\) of \(G\) such that when the group operation of \(G\) is restricted to \(H\), \(H\) is a group in its own right.
We write \(H \leq G\).
A subgroup uses the same operation as the original group.
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Complex Numbers and Operations
The complex numbers are defined as
\[
\mathbb{C}=\{a+bi:a,b\in\mathbb{R}\},
\]
where \(i^2=-1\). If \(z=a+bi\), then \(a\) is the real part of \(z\) and \(b\) is the imaginary part of \(z\).
If \(z=a+bi\) and \(w=c+di\), then
\[
z+w=(a+c)+(b+d)i.
\]
Multiplication is given by
\[
zw=(a+bi)(c+di)=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i.
\]
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Multiplicative Inverses and Conjugates
Every nonzero complex number \(z=a+bi\) has a multiplicative inverse:
\[
z^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}.
\]
The complex conjugate of \(z=a+bi\) is
\[
\overline{z}=a-bi.
\]
The absolute value or modulus of \(z=a+bi\) is \(|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\).
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Examples
For example, if \(z=2+3i\), then
\[
z^{-1}=\frac{2}{13}-\frac{3}{13}i,
\qquad |z|=\sqrt{13},
\qquad \overline{z}=2-3i.
\]
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Polar representation of Complex Numbers
Nonzero complex numbers can also be represented using polar coordinates.
\(z=a+bi=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\) where \(a=r\cos\theta\) and \(b=r\sin\theta\), and \(r=|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\).
Book abbreviates \(r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\) as \(r\operatorname{cis}\theta\).
We require \(0\leq\theta<2\pi\).

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
\(n^{\text{th}}\) Roots of Unity
The complex numbers satisfying the equation
\[
z^n=1
\]
are called the \(n\)th roots of unity.
They lie on the unit circle and are equally spaced around the circle.
A generator for the group of the \(n\)th roots of unity is called a primitive \(n\)th root of unity.
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Theorem 4.2.10
If \(z^n=1\), then the \(n\)th roots of unity are
\[
z=\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{2k\pi}{n}\right),
\]
where \(k=0,1,\ldots,n-1\).
Furthermore, the \(n\)th roots of unity form a cyclic subgroup of \(\mathbb{T}\) of order \(n\).
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Proof
By DeMoivre’s Theorem,
\[
z^n
=\operatorname{cis}\left(n\frac{2k\pi}{n}\right)
=\operatorname{cis}(2k\pi)
=1.
\]
crumbs: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers

title: Slides: Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
text:
Example 9th roots of unity
The \(9\)th roots of unity satisfy
\[
z^9=1.
\]
By Theorem 4.2.10,
\[
z_k=\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{2k\pi}{9}\right),
\qquad k=0,1,\ldots,8.
\]
Thus the nine roots are
\[
1,\;
\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}{9}\right),\;
\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{4\pi}{9}\right),\;
\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{6\pi}{9}\right),\;
\ldots,\;
\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{16\pi}{9}\right).
\]
They form a cyclic subgroup of \(\mathbb{T}\) of order \(9\).
For example,
\[
\omega=\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{2\pi}{9}\right)
\]
is a primitive \(9\)th root of unity, and
\[
\langle\omega\rangle
=\{1,\omega,\omega^2,\ldots,\omega^8\}.
\]

Definition of a Group
A group \((G,\cdot)\) is a set \(G\) together with a law of composition
\((a,b)\mapsto a\cdot b\) satisfying:

Associativity:
\((a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)\) for \(a,b,c\in G\).
Identity:
There exists \(e\in G\) such that \(e\cdot a=a\cdot e=a\) for every \(a\in G\).
Inverses:
For each \(a\in G\), there exists \(a^{-1}\in G\) such that \(a\cdot a^{-1}=a^{-1}\cdot a=e\).

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Definition of a Subgroup
Let \(G\) be a group.
A subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) is a subset \(H\) of \(G\) such that when the group operation of \(G\) is restricted to \(H\), \(H\) is a group in its own right.
We write \(H \leq G\).
A subgroup uses the same operation as the original group.

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Definition of Cosets
Let \(G\) be a group and \(H\) a subgroup of \(G\).
A left coset of \(H\) with representative \(g \in G\) is the set
\(gH = \{gh : h \in H\}\).
A right coset is defined similarly by
\(Hg = \{hg : h \in H\}\).
If left and right cosets coincide, or if it is clear from context which type of coset is meant, we simply use the word coset.

Theorem 6.1.4
Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a group \(G\).
Then the left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\) partition \(G\).

That is, the group \(G\) is the disjoint union of the left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\).

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Proof of 6.1.4
Different proof from the book. Define a relation on \(G\) by \(g_1 \sim g_2\) if and only if \(g_1^{-1}g_2 \in H\). I will show this is an equivalence relation.

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Remark 6.1.5
There is nothing special about left cosets. Right cosets also partition \(G\). The proof is the same as for left cosets, except that all group multiplications are done on the opposite side of \(H\).

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Theorem 6.1.8
Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a group \(G\).
The number of left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\) is the same as the number of
right cosets of \(H\) in \(G\).

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Proof Idea
Let \(L_H\) and \(R_H\) denote the sets of left and right
cosets of \(H\), respectively.
Define \(\phi\:L_H\to R_H\) by \(\phi(gH)=Hg^{-1}\).
Lemma 6.1.3 shows that \(\phi\) is well-defined and one-to-one.
It is onto since \(\phi(g^{-1}H)=Hg\).
Therefore \(\phi\) is a bijection, so the number of left and right cosets
is the same.

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Proposition 6.2.1
Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\) with \(g\in G\) and define a map \(\phi:H\rightarrow gH\) by \(\phi(h)=gh\).
The map \(\phi\) is bijective; hence, the number of elements in \(H\) is the same as the number of elements in \(gH\).

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Proposition 6.2.1 Proof
We first show that the map \(\phi\) is one-to-one.
Suppose that \(\phi(h_1)=\phi(h_2)\) for elements \(h_1,h_2\in H\).
We must show that \(h_1=h_2\), but \(\phi(h_1)=gh_1\) and \(\phi(h_2)=gh_2\).
So \(gh_1=gh_2\), and by left cancellation \(h_1=h_2\).

To show that \(\phi\) is onto is easy.
By definition every element of \(gH\) is of the form \(gh\) for some \(h\in H\) and \(\phi(h)=gh\).

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Lagrange’s Theorem
Let \(G\) be a finite group and let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\).
Then \(|G|/|H|=[G:H]\) is the number of distinct left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\).
In particular, the number of elements in \(H\) must divide the number of elements in \(G\).

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Lagrange’s Theorem Proof
The group \(G\) is partitioned into \([G:H]\) distinct left cosets.
Each left coset has \(|H|\) elements; therefore,
\[
|G|=[G:H]|H|.
\]

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Corollary 6.2.3
Suppose that \(G\) is a finite group and \(g\in G\).
Then the order of \(g\) must divide the number of elements in \(G\).

Proof. Apply Lagrange’s Theorem to the subgroup \(\langle g\rangle\).
The order of \(g\) is \(|\langle g\rangle|\), so \(|\langle g\rangle|\) divides \(|G|\).

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Corollary 6.2.4
Let \(|G|=p\) with \(p\) a prime number.
Then \(G\) is cyclic and any \(g\in G\) such that \(g\neq e\) is a generator.

Proof. Let \(g\) be in \(G\) such that \(g\neq e\).
Then by Corollary 6.2.3, the order of \(g\) must divide the order of the group.
Since \(|\langle g\rangle|>1\), it must be \(p\).
Hence, \(g\) generates \(G\).

title: Slides: Coset flavored vegetables
text:
Corollary 6.2.5
Let \(H\) and \(K\) be subgroups of a finite group \(G\) such that \(G\supset H\supset K\).
Then \([G:K]=[G:H][H:K]\).

Proof. Observe that
\[
[G:K]
=\frac{|G|}{|K|}
=\frac{|G|}{|H|}\cdot\frac{|H|}{|K|}
=[G:H][H:K].
\]

The group \(A_4\) has no subgroup of order \(6\).

The converse of Lagrange’s Theorem is false.
Although \(6\) divides \(|A_4|=12\), there is no subgroup of \(A_4\) of order \(6\).

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Subgroups of Index 2
Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\) with \([G:H]=2\). There are only two left cosets and two right cosets: \(H\) and its complement in \(G\).
Thus \(gH=Hg\) for every \(g\in G\), or equivalently,
\[
gHg^{-1}=H.
\]

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Proposition 6.2.7
The group \(A_4\) has no subgroup of order \(6\).

Suppose \(|H|=6\). Then \([A_4:H]=2\), so \(gHg^{-1}=H\) for every \(g\in A_4\).
Of the eight \(3\)-cycles in \(A_4\), at least one lies in \(H\). We may take it to be \((123)\). Its inverse \((132)\) also lies in \(H\).
Conjugating by elements of \(A_4\) gives \((243)\) and \((142)\). Their inverses must also lie in \(H\). Together with the identity, these are seven distinct elements, contradicting \(|H|=6\).


The converse of Lagrange’s Theorem is false: \(6\) divides \(|A_4|=12\), but \(A_4\) has no subgroup of order \(6\).

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Corollary
If \(G\) is a finite group and \(g\in G\), then
\[
g^{|G|}=e.
\]
The order of \(g\) divides \(|G|\), so \(|G|=k|g|\) for some integer \(k\). Hence \(g^{|G|}=(g^{|g|})^k=e\).

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
The Group \(U(n)\)
\(U(n)\) is the group of units in \(\mathbb{Z}_n\) under multiplication modulo \(n\):
\[
U(n)=\{[a]\in\mathbb{Z}_n:\gcd(a,n)=1\}.
\]
For example, \(U(12)=\{[1],[5],[7],[11]\}\).
Each element has a multiplicative inverse modulo \(n\). For instance, \([5][5]=[1]\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\).

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Euler’s Phi Function
The Euler \(\phi\)-function is the map \(\phi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\) defined by \(\phi(1)=1\) and, for \(n>1\),
\[
\phi(n)=|\{m:1\leq m<n,\ \gcd(m,n)=1\}|.
\]
For example, \(\phi(12)=4\) because \(1,5,7,11\) are relatively prime to \(12\).
If \(p\) is prime, then \(\phi(p)=p-1\).

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Theorem 6.3.1
Let \(U(n)\) be the group of units in \(\mathbb{Z}_n\). Then
\[
|U(n)|=\phi(n).
\]
The units are precisely the residue classes represented by integers relatively prime to \(n\).

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Euler’s Theorem
Let \(a\) and \(n\) be integers such that \(n>0\) and \(\gcd(a,n)=1\). Then
\[
a^{\phi(n)}\equiv 1\pmod n.
\]

The residue class of \(a\) belongs to \(U(n)\), which has order \(\phi(n)\). Applying the preceding corollary in \(U(n)\) proves the congruence.

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Fermat’s Little Theorem
Let \(p\) be prime. If \(p\nmid a\), then
\[
a^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]
Furthermore, for any integer \(b\),
\[
b^p\equiv b\pmod p.
\]

text:
Conjugation
For \(g,h\in G\), the element \(ghg^{-1}\) is the conjugate of \(h\) by \(g\).
For a subgroup \(H\) of \(G\), write \(gHg^{-1}=\{ghg^{-1}:h\in H\}\).

Conjugating a cycle applies the conjugating permutation to each entry:
\[
\sigma(a_1\,a_2\,\ldots\,a_k)\sigma^{-1}
=(\sigma(a_1)\,\sigma(a_2)\,\ldots\,\sigma(a_k)).
\]
For example, \((124)(123)(124)^{-1}=(243)\).

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Theorem 6.2.8
Two cycles \(\tau\) and \(\mu\) in \(S_n\) have the same length if and only if there exists a \(\sigma\in S_n\) such that
\[
\mu=\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}.
\]

If \(\tau=(a_1\,\ldots\,a_k)\) and \(\mu=(b_1\,\ldots\,b_k)\), choose \(\sigma\) with \(\sigma(a_i)=b_i\) for each \(i\), then extend it to a permutation of the remaining symbols.
Conversely, conjugating \(\tau\) replaces its entries by their images under \(\sigma\), preserving the cycle length.

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Conjugation Is an Equivalence Relation
Define \(h\sim k\) when \(k=ghg^{-1}\) for some \(g\in G\).

Reflexive: \(h=ehe^{-1}\).
Symmetric: If \(k=ghg^{-1}\), then \(h=g^{-1}kg\).
Transitive: If \(k=ghg^{-1}\) and \(\ell=aka^{-1}\), then \(\ell=(ag)h(ag)^{-1}\).

The equivalence classes are called conjugacy classes.

section: Conjugacy Classes and the Center of a Group
text:
Conjugacy Classes and the Center of a Group
The center of a group \(G\) is the set \(Z(G)=\{g\in G:gh=hg\text{ for all }h\in G\}\).
What is can you say about the conjugacy classes of elements in \(Z(G)\)?

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
section: Class Equation and Conjugacy Classes in \(S_n\)
text:
Class Equation and Conjugacy Classes in \(S_n\)
Conjugacy classes partition a finite group \(G\). If \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\) represent its classes outside the center, the class equation is
\[
|G|=|Z(G)|+|[x_1]|+\cdots+|[x_k]|.
\]

In \(S_n\), permutations are conjugate exactly when they have the same cycle type. If a permutation has \(m_j\) cycles of length \(j\), including fixed points, then
\[
|[\sigma]|=\frac{n!}{\prod_{j=1}^{n}j^{m_j}m_j!}.
\]

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Class Sizes and Centralizers
For \(x\in G\), its centralizer is \(C_G(x)=\{g\in G:gx=xg\}\).
The conjugacy class of \(x\) has size
\[
|[x]|=[G:C_G(x)]=\frac{|G|}{|C_G(x)|}.
\]

In \(S_4\), the permutations commuting with \((123)\) are \((1)\), \((123)\), and \((132)\). Thus
\[
|[(123)]|=\frac{24}{3}=8.
\]

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
The Center of a Finite \(p\)-Group
Theorem. If \(|G|=p^n\) for a prime \(p\), then \(Z(G)\) contains an element other than the identity.

Each conjugacy class outside \(Z(G)\) has size greater than \(1\) and divides \(p^n\). Its size is therefore divisible by \(p\).
The class equation gives
\[
p^n=|Z(G)|+\sum_i |[x_i]|.
\]
It follows that \(p\) divides \(|Z(G)|\). Since \(e\in Z(G)\), we have \(|Z(G)|\geq p\).

title: Slides: Fermat and Euler’s Theorems
text:
Groups of Order \(p^2\)
Corollary. Every group of order \(p^2\) is abelian.

The preceding theorem and Lagrange’s Theorem give \(|Z(G)|=p\) or \(p^2\).
Suppose \(|Z(G)|=p\) and choose \(x\notin Z(G)\). The centralizer \(C_G(x)\) contains both \(Z(G)\) and \(x\), so it has more than \(p\) elements. Its order divides \(p^2\), forcing \(C_G(x)=G\).
But then \(x\in Z(G)\), a contradiction. Hence \(Z(G)=G\), so \(G\) is abelian.

Definition: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\). The centralizer of \(H\) in \(G\) is
\(C_G(H) = \{g \in G : gh = hg \text{ for all } h \in H\}\).

if \(H = \{x\}\), we write \(C_G(x)\) for \(C_G(H)\).
\(C_G(G) = Z(G)\).

title: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes
text:
Centralizers Are Subgroups
Proposition: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\). Then \(C_G(H)\) is a subgroup of \(G\).

Proof:

Since \(eh = he\) for every \(h \in H\), we have \(e \in C_G(H)\).
Suppose \(a,b \in C_G(H)\). For every \(h \in H\),
\[(ab)h = a(bh) = a(hb) = (ah)b = (ha)b = h(ab).\]
Suppose \(a \in C_G(H)\). Since \(ah = ha\) for every \(h \in H\), we have \(a^{-1}h = ha^{-1}\).

title: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes
text:
Conjugation
For \(g,h\in G\), the element \(ghg^{-1}\) is the conjugate of \(h\) by \(g\).
For a subgroup \(H\) of \(G\), write \(gHg^{-1}=\{ghg^{-1}:h\in H\}\).
Conjugation is a an equivalence relation on \(G\) where \(x \sim y\) if and only if \(y = gxg^{-1}\) for some \(g \in G\).
The equivalence classes are called conjugacy classes
crumbs: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes

title: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes
text:
Class Equation
\[G=Z(G)\cup [x_1]\cup [x_2]\cup\cdots\cup [x_k],\]
where \([x_i]\) are the conjugacy classes of \(G\) outside the center. \([x_i]=\{gx_ig^{-1}:g\in G\}\)
If \(x\in Z(G)\), then \([x]=\{x\}\), since \(gxg^{-1}=x\) for all \(g\in G\).

title: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes
text:
Class Sizes and Centralizers
Proposition: For \(x\in G\), its centralizer is \(C_G(x)=\{g\in G:gx=xg\}\).
The conjugacy class of \(x\) has size
\[
|[x]|=[G:C_G(x)]=\frac{|G|}{|C_G(x)|}.
\]

title: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes
text:
Proof of Class Size Formula
Consider the map \(\phi\) from the set of cosets of \(C_G(x)\) in \(G\) to the conjugacy class of \(x\) defined by \[
\phi(gC_G(x))=g x g^{-1}.
\]
Need to show that \(\phi\) is well-defined, injective, and surjective.

title: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes
text:
Class Equation Updated
\[|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum_i |G:C_G(x_i)|=|Z(G)|+\sum_i \frac{|G|}{|C_G(x_i)|}\]
where \(x_i\) are representatives of the conjugacy classes outside the center.
crumbs: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes

title: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes
text:
The Center of a Finite \(p\)-Group
Theorem. If \(|G|=p^n\) for a prime \(p\), then \(Z(G)\) contains an element other than the identity.

Each conjugacy class outside \(Z(G)\) has size greater than \(1\) and divides \(p^n\). Its size is therefore divisible by \(p\).
The class equation gives
\[
p^n=|Z(G)|+\sum_i |[x_i]|.
\]
It follows that \(p\) divides \(|Z(G)|\). Since \(e\in Z(G)\), we have \(|Z(G)|\geq p\).
crumbs: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes

title: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes
text:
Groups of Order \(p^2\)
Corollary. Every group of order \(p^2\) is abelian.

The preceding theorem and Lagrange’s Theorem give \(|Z(G)|=p\) or \(p^2\).
Suppose \(|Z(G)|=p\) and choose \(x\notin Z(G)\). The centralizer \(C_G(x)\) contains both \(Z(G)\) and \(x\), so it has more than \(p\) elements. Its order divides \(p^2\), forcing \(C_G(x)=G\).
But then \(x\in Z(G)\), a contradiction. Hence \(Z(G)=G\), so \(G\) is abelian.

List the elements of \(A_4\) by cycle type. Which \(S_4\) conjugacy classes split when conjugation is restricted to elements of \(A_4\)?

Let

Therefore the conjugacy classes are
\[
\{e\},\qquad
\{r,r^4\},\qquad
\{r^2,r^3\},\qquad
\{s,rs,r^2s,r^3s,r^4s\},
\]

10=1+2+2+5.

title: Slides: Centralizers, Centers, and Conjugacy Classes
section: Class Equation and Conjugacy Classes in \(S_n\)
text:
Class Equation and Conjugacy Classes in \(S_n\)
Conjugacy classes partition a finite group \(G\). If \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\) represent its classes outside the center, the class equation is
\[
|G|=|Z(G)|+|[x_1]|+\cdots+|[x_k]|.
\]

In \(S_n\), permutations are conjugate exactly when they have the same cycle type. If a permutation has \(m_j\) cycles of length \(j\), including fixed points, then
\[
|[\sigma]|=\frac{n!}{\prod_{j=1}^{n}j^{m_j}m_j!}.
\]

Basically what this boils down to is: the work that you submit for credit should be your own work and reflect your understanding of the course material. Group work, collaborations, and the free exchange of ideas are fundamental aspects of an academic environment. I encourage you all to talk and work with others in the class, as it will enhance your understanding of the material. You must write up your assignment individually and explain solutions in your own words. It is also important to cite resources you used in work, these may include other students, books, websites, and instructors.
There is a distinction between collaboration and copying. Collaboration is encouraged; copying solutions or assignments is not allowed. If I find copying of solutions on an assignment it will result in a score of 0 on that assignment. Multiple instances of academic dishonesty will be formally documented with the University.
